Hey hey [laugh], how's it goin', thanks for jumping on.
[concerned tone] Ok so I actually wanted to jump straight into this 'cause we've got a bit of a situation with host cancellations here at Airbnb.
You good ta follow along while I walk through everything?
[inhale] So basically, our whole marketplace is built on trust, right, and when a host cancels a confirmed booking it's a TOTAL disaster for the guest who thought they had a place to stay, and it's a MASSIVE headache for our support teams who gotta scramble ta fix it.
[thoughtful] Sooo I went through the data, and... it looks like the host cancellation rate, which is just the percent of confirmed bookings that hosts back out of, has actually spiked from ELEVEN PERCENT to FOURTEEN PERCENT in just the last six months, and like, that climb is what's really alarming.
I think hosts are running into a buncha friction, you know, like calendar conflicts or pricing mistakes, and they just like bail on the reservation, and here's the kicker, every single one of those cancellations costs us around TWENTY EIGHT DOLLARS in support, relocation, and refunds.
[worried tone] And when you add all that up across the whole platform, it's costing us over NINE MILLION DOLLARS a year in operational costs, 'cause we gotta manually step in, rebook guests, and hand out refunds, so we're basically just burning money on customer support instead of growing the community... [pause] all this make sense?
[concerned tone] Ok cool.
So yeah, it's a pretty big problem that's hitting a lot of our guests and hosts.
[excited] And if we're gonna fix it, we gotta know what success actually looks like, so let's lock onto two main targets, alright?
[confident] So the first one is that host cancellation rate, we wanna get that down from FOURTEEN PERCENT to TEN PERCENT, that's the bar, and basically lower is better 'cause it means fewer guests getting stranded and fewer fires for our team ta put out.
And the second target is the money, we should be aiming for at least THREE MILLION DOLLARS in annual operational savings, 'cause right now we're bleeding over nine million a year and that's just WAYY too high, you know what I mean?
[sincere] So like, what I really wanna avoid is just talking about the problem without actually moving the needle on the money, so let's stay laser focused on those two things, the rate down ta ten percent AND that three million in savings, and if we hit both, we KNOW it worked.
Make sense?
Okay, so before we get into the roadmap, I want to show you what the finished deliverable should actually look like — because having a concrete target in your head makes everything that follows a lot easier.
What you're building is a Final Operational Proposal — and I want to use this Uber carpool pricing proposal as the reference, because it's a really clean example of the same type of document: one operational problem, one recommendation, and a financial case that justifies it.
The document opens with an executive summary, and this is the most important section — it's the one thing a busy VP will actually read in full.
Notice how it leads with the cost right away — it says 'A pricing misalignment is costing us $42M a year.' That's not buried on page five, it's the very first sentence — the problem, the scale, and the stakes, all in one line.
Then it immediately follows with the recommendation and the projected recovery range — $14M to $18M — so the reader knows the answer before they've read a single page of analysis.
For your proposal, the same logic applies — your exec summary should state the 11% to 14% spike, the $9M annual cost, and your one recommendation upfront, before anything else.
After the summary, the document spends real estate proving the problem — and this maps directly to the trend analysis you'll need to build.
Look at how it's structured: monthly ride data from October through March, broken down by market tier and time of day — not just one headline number, but the trend over time and where it's concentrated.
That's the pattern you want to follow — show the overall cancellation rate moving from 11% to 14%, then break it down by listing type and region so you can show where the problem is actually hitting hardest.
Once the trend is established, the document identifies a single primary driver — and that's exactly what your proposal needs to do too.
What makes this section strong is that it doesn't just name the cause — it quantifies the damage per unit. It says solo unmatched rides cost negative $3.55 per ride across 5.21 million rides a month — so you can see exactly how the $42M figure is built up from the ground.
Your version needs the same thing — once you've identified the primary cancellation driver, show the $28 per-cancellation cost, multiply it through the volume, and build up to that $9M annual figure so the reader can follow the math.
The proposal section is where everything comes together — and the key thing to notice is that there is exactly one recommendation, not a list of options.
And it's tied directly to the root cause — because the problem was the flat discount model, the fix is a dynamic one. Your recommendation needs that same direct link: whatever driver you identify, your solution should target it specifically.
Then on the impact side, the document shows a base case and a conservative case — match rate goes from 38% to 55%, and annual recovery lands between $14M and $18M. You need the same structure: a projected savings figure aiming for that $3M target, with the assumptions spelled out so it's credible.
So the through-line of the whole document is: here's the trend, here's what's driving it, here's what it's costing, here's the one fix, and here's what we get back — and every section earns its place by moving that story forward.
Keep that structure in mind as we walk through the process, because each step you're about to do maps pretty cleanly onto one of those sections.
[thoughtful] Perfect, perfect.
Okay so here's basically how we're gonna get there, nothing tooo crazy, but I want you ta see the roadmap so you know where we're headed.
So first, you're gonna build a host cancellation trend analysis, and I'll send over a file with a buncha booking data from the last six months, and you'll quantify how big this thing is, like looking at the overall cancellation rate, the monthly trends, and the rates broken down by listing type and region so we can see WHERE it's coming from.
Then second, you'll move into the root cause analysis, which is just where you figure out the REAL reason hosts are canceling, so you'll segment the data and dig into stuff like pricing mistakes or calendar conflicts ta see which one underlying issue is driving most of the spike.
After that, once we've got the why, you'll build out a cancellation cost model ta map the damage and show exactly how that nine million breaks down, and then finally you'll land on exactly ONE operational recommendation, like maybe better calendar tools or stricter policies, we'll figure out what the data points to.
And all of that rolls up into the big deliverable, which is the Final Operational Proposal, a clean doc, PDF or Doc, and a good one's gotta show that trend from eleven to fourteen percent, name the primary cancellation driver, lay out that nine million dollar cost, and give exactly one fix with projected savings aiming at three million.
[curious] Sound like a plan?
[excited] Okayy cool, glad the plan's clear.
I know it feels like a lot with the financial analysis and all that data, but honestly we're just building one solid recommendation ta save the company some serious money.
[pause] I just got a few quick questions ta make sure we're aligned on all this... [curious] you ready?

panels.headline:
Host cancellations are
bleeding us dry.
panels.key_visual: Cover slide with bold claim headline and speaker attribution. .cover .big holds the hook, .cover .sub shows 'Jay Shah, Operations Lead'. .pillnote held element (id='pill-cover') reveals with 'Six months. Fourteen percent. Nine million lost.'

panels.headline: The marketplace runs on trust.
panels.key_visual: Single bold statement. .statement u fades in on panel activate. No sub-line — the narrator explains the trust foundation verbatim.

panels.headline: One cancel is a total disaster.
panels.key_visual: Single statement emphasizing the guest impact. .statement u on panel open. Second statement (id='stat2-b2-2') held, reveals with 'MASSIVE headache for our support teams who gotta scramble ta fix it.'

panels.headline: The rate climbed fast.
panels.key_visual: Trend chart with SVG polyline (id='trendline'). Axis labels '6 months ago' at 11%, 'today' at 14%. .chart u wraps the SVG. Line draws from left (11%) to right (14%) via draw_line cue on end-value anchor. Use var(--bad) stroke for worsening trend.

panels.headline: Two suspects. No evidence yet.
panels.key_visual: Two suspect cards reveal sequentially. sc-1: 'Calendar conflicts' with description 'Hosts double-booked or unavailable'. sc-2: 'Pricing mistakes' with description 'Rates set too low to fulfill'. Each card has question mark icon and fires on its own probe.

Giant number in white (no semantic color — cost is stated neutrally in narration). .num u on panel activate. No sub-line — narrator says 'every single one of those cancellations costs us around TWENTY EIGHT DOLLARS in support, relocation, and refunds' verbatim.

panels.headline: $9M+
panels.key_visual: Giant bad number showing annual cost. .num.bad u. No sub-line — narrator explains 'over NINE MILLION DOLLARS a year in operational costs' and the breakdown immediately after.

panels.headline:
We're burning money on support
instead of growing the community.
panels.key_visual: Two-clause statement with dual emphasis. .statement u on panel open. No secondary element — the contrast is in the headline itself.

panels.headline: Let's lock onto two main targets.
panels.key_visual: Section opener. .statement u. No sub-line — narrator immediately names the targets in the next breath.

panels.headline: Cut the rate.
panels.key_visual: Flow panel: 14% (bad) → 10% (good). .flow u with .fnum.bad on left, .pill 'cut to', .fnum.good on right. No sub-line — narrator says 'get that down from FOURTEEN PERCENT to TEN PERCENT' verbatim.

panels.headline: $3M
panels.key_visual: Giant good number showing savings target. .num.good u. No sub-line — narrator explains 'at least THREE MILLION DOLLARS in annual operational savings' and the rationale immediately after.

panels.headline: Two numbers decide this.
panels.key_visual: Two KPI columns. .statement u as headline. cc-1 (bad): 'KPI 1' label, 'Cancellation rate' title. cc-2 (good): 'KPI 2' label, 'Operational savings' title. Each column reveals on its own probe.

panels.headline: Here's the roadmap.
panels.key_visual: Section opener. .statement u. No sub-line — narrator says 'so you know where we're headed' immediately after.

panels.headline: Four stages from data to fix.
panels.key_visual: Four-cell plan grid. pc-1: '01' 'Trend analysis' 'Six-month cancellation rate by cohort'. pc-2: '02' 'Root cause' 'Segment by reason code'. pc-3: '03' 'Cost model' 'Map the $9M breakdown'. pc-4: '04' 'Recommendation' 'One operational fix with projected savings'. Each cell reveals on its own probe as narrator names that stage.

panels.headline:
Final Operational Proposal.
One doc. Save $3M.
panels.key_visual: .deliv u with multi-line headline. No sub-line — narrator explains the deliverable format and contents verbatim in the following sentences.

panels.headline: A good one shows all four.
panels.key_visual: Four checklist rows. ck-1: 'Trend from 11% to 14%'. ck-2: 'Primary cancellation driver'. ck-3: '$9M cost breakdown'. ck-4: 'One fix with $3M savings projection'. Each row reveals as narrator names that requirement.

panels.headline:
One solid recommendation.
Serious money saved.
panels.key_visual: .statement u. No sub-line — narrator says 'we're just building one solid recommendation ta save the company some serious money' verbatim.

panels.headline: Let's get after it.
panels.key_visual: Final hero panel. .fill gradient background. .statement u with large display headline. Wordmark turns white on .fill.
